content: Adenomyosis is a medical condition where endometrial tissue, which normally lines the inner cavity of the uterus, is found within the myometrium, the thick muscular layer of the uterus. This condition is most commonly observed in women aged 35 to 50. Patients with adenomyosis often experience painful menstruation (dysmenorrhea) and/or heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia). The condition can affect the uterus either diffusely, leading to a bulky and heavier uterus, or focally, forming a localized mass called an adenomyoma. Adenomyosis was first identified in 1860 by Carl von Rokitansky, a German pathologist, who described the presence of endometrial glands within the myometrium. He referred to this finding as cystosarcoma adenoids uterinum. In 1892, Thomas Stephen Cullen, a gynecologist, conducted the first systematic study of adenomyosis and classified adenomyomas into three types: intramural, subperitoneal, and submucous. Cullen also proposed the mucosal theory, suggesting that endometrial tissue invades the myometrium through small fissures. He later recommended abdominal hysterectomy as a treatment, as the endometrial growths are interwoven with the uterine muscle. Adenomyosis can be classified histopathologically into two main types: diffuse adenomyosis, characterized by a uniformly enlarged and boggy uterus, and focal adenomyosis (adenomyoma), which resembles a fibroid but lacks a surrounding pseudocapsule. Another variant, juvenile cystic adenomyosis, involves endometrial cysts larger than 1 cm within the myometrium and is typically seen in women under 30 years of age. The exact pathogenesis of adenomyosis remains poorly understood. Two main theories have been proposed: (1) invagination of the endometrium into the myometrium due to uterine smooth muscle weakness, and (2) de novo development of adenomyosis from Müllerian remnants through metaplasia. Additionally, the basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF) receptor/ligand system is upregulated in adenomyosis, contributing to abnormal uterine bleeding and menorrhagia. Hormones such as estrogen and progesterone, as well as oxytocin, FSH, and prolactin, also play a role in the disease's pathogenesis. Gross pathology reveals a globular enlargement of the myometrium with cysts containing hemolyzed red blood cells and sideroblasts. Microscopically, endometrial glands and stroma are surrounded by hypertrophic smooth muscle bundles scattered within the myometrium. The cause of adenomyosis is unknown, but it has been associated with uterine trauma that disrupts the barrier between the endometrium and myometrium, such as cesarean sections, tubal ligation, abortion, or pregnancy. Adenomyosis is estimated to affect 20-35% of women, though its true prevalence is difficult to determine due to diagnostic limitations. It is more commonly diagnosed in women aged 40-50 undergoing hysterectomy and less frequently in adolescents undergoing pelvic imaging. There is no racial predilection for adenomyosis, and it is most often observed in multiparous women, though no definitive causal relationship has been established between multiparity and the disease. Risk factors for adenomyosis are not well-defined, as diagnosis typically requires pathological examination of hysterectomy specimens. The condition often coexists with other pelvic diseases, such as endometriosis and leiomyoma, making it unclear whether it has specific risk factors. Prior uterine surgery may be a potential risk factor. Early clinical features of adenomyosis include dysmenorrhea, heavy menstrual bleeding, and chronic pelvic pain. Complications may include preterm birth and miscarriage in younger women diagnosed via pelvic imaging. The relationship between adenomyosis and infertility remains controversial. Prognosis is generally favorable, as hysterectomy is often curative unless other uterine pathologies are present. There is no increased risk of developing endometrial carcinoma secondary to adenomyosis. Adenomyosis is primarily a histopathological diagnosis made after hysterectomy. Preoperative diagnosis is suggested by pelvic imaging, such as transvaginal ultrasound or MRI, combined with symptoms like heavy menstrual bleeding, dysmenorrhea, and a uniformly enlarged, globular uterus. Symptoms of adenomyosis include heavy menstrual bleeding, dysmenorrhea, and chronic pelvic pain. On physical examination, a bimanual pelvic exam may reveal a diffusely enlarged, boggy, and mobile uterus with uterine tenderness. Pelvic imaging, including ultrasound and MRI, is used to evaluate the uterus. Transvaginal ultrasound is the most cost-effective and widely available modality, showing a heterogeneous uterine texture without the well-defined masses seen in fibroids. MRI offers superior diagnostic capability due to its higher spatial and contrast resolution and is particularly useful in differentiating adenomyosis from multiple small uterine fibroids. MRI findings include diffuse or focal thickening of the junctional zone (>12 mm) with areas of low signal intensity and occasional bright foci on T2-weighted images, corresponding to ectopic endometrial tissue and cystic gland dilation. Treatment for adenomyosis primarily involves surgery. Hysterectomy, with preservation of the ovaries, is the most common approach and can be performed via abdominal, transvaginal, laparoscopic, or robotic methods. Unlike leiomyomas, adenomyomas cannot be excised with a clear cleavage plane, making uterus-sparing resection an investigational approach, particularly for young women desiring future pregnancy. Medical therapy can be used as a temporary option for young women in the childbearing period to manage symptoms like dysmenorrhea and menorrhagia. Hormonal treatments include levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine devices (IUDs), combined oral contraceptives, GnRH analogs, and oral GnRH antagonists. Levonorgestrel-IUDs act directly on the uterus to alleviate symptoms but are not curative, as symptoms typically recur within six months of discontinuing hormonal therapy.
